title: Chapter 1 (Life Section): What Life Insurance Involves

cards.title: What is an Asset?
cards.content: An asset is a kind of property which yields certain value. Every asset has two features: (1) It has an Economic Value. (2) It provides a Benefit or Income to its owner. Examples: House, Car, Human Life, Plant and Machinery.

cards.title: What is NOT an Asset? (Exam Trap)
cards.content: Air and Sunlight are NOT assets. They are natural gifts provided equally to everyone — rich or poor — by nature. No individual can claim personal ownership of air or sunlight. They have no personal economic value that can be insured.

sections.title: 💡 Human Life Value (HLV) — The Most Important Concept

cards.title: What is HLV?
cards.content: HLV stands for Human Life Value. It is a traditional method that determines how much insurance is needed by an individual. Different people earn different incomes, so every person's life has a different financial value — and HLV helps calculate the correct insurance amount for each person.

cards.title: Who Introduced the HLV Concept?
cards.content: The concept of Human Life Value (HLV) was introduced by Professor S.S. Huebner. This is a frequently asked exam question. Note: The correct spelling is 'Huebner' — not 'Habner' as sometimes misspelled.

sections.title: ⚠️ Three Types of Risk in Human Life

cards.title: 1. Dying Too Early
cards.content: If a person dies at a young age (premature death), it is a major financial risk for the family. The family loses its income source suddenly, causing financial hardship. This is covered under Life Insurance.

cards.title: 2. Living Too Long
cards.content: If a person lives for a very long time beyond their earning years (typically up to age 60), they become financially dependent on others. The risk of outliving one's income is also categorized as a risk in Life Insurance.

cards.title: 3. Living with Disability
cards.content: If a person lives with a permanent or partial disability, their ability to earn income is reduced or eliminated. This is also treated as a risk category in Life Insurance because financial help is greatly needed.

cards.title: ⚠️ What is NOT a Risk? — Natural Wear and Tear
cards.content: Natural Wear and Tear refers to the gradual deterioration that occurs naturally over time — for example, a person aging, a machine becoming old, or a car losing value over time. This is NOT considered a risk and is NOT covered under any insurance policy.

sections.title: 🔄 Life Insurance vs General Insurance — Key Difference

cards.title: Life Insurance = Contract of Assurance
cards.content: A Life Insurance policy is a Contract of Assurance. 'Assurance' means certainty or guarantee. The event (death) is certain to happen — only the timing is uncertain. Therefore, the insurer assures the payment to the policyholder or nominee.

cards.title: General Insurance = Contract of Indemnity
cards.content: General Insurance policies (Motor, Health, Fire, etc.) are Contracts of Indemnity. 'Indemnity' means compensation for actual loss. These policies compensate only the actual amount of loss suffered. If no loss occurs, the policy expires and must be renewed each year.

cards.title: Common Trap in Exam
cards.content: The exam may REVERSE the definitions: 'Life Insurance = Indemnity, General = Assurance.' This is WRONG. Always remember: Life = Assurance, General = Indemnity.

sections.title: 📊 Age and Premium — Why Young People Pay Less

cards.title: Mortality is Related to Age
cards.content: Mortality means death rate. As age increases, the risk of death also increases — a person gets closer to death with each passing year. Therefore, older individuals are charged higher life insurance premiums because they carry a greater risk of dying sooner.

cards.title: Key Formula to Remember
cards.content: Higher Age = Higher Mortality Risk = Higher Premium. Lower Age = Lower Mortality Risk = Lower Premium. This is directly related to age — mortality and age have a direct (positive) relationship.

sections.title: 💰 Cash Value Insurance Contract — Advantages and Disadvantages

cards.title: Advantages (What Cash Value Insurance DOES offer)
cards.content: 1. Safe and Secure Investment — money is protected. 2. Inculcates Saving Discipline — forces the policyholder to save regularly through premium payments. 3. Income Tax Advantage — premiums paid qualify for tax benefits under the Income Tax Act.

cards.title: Disadvantage (What Cash Value Insurance does NOT offer)
cards.content: Lower Yields — the returns from life insurance policies are generally lower compared to market-linked investments. This is a disadvantage, not an advantage. Do not confuse this with the advantages listed above.

sections.title: 👨👩👧 Family Floater Policy and Life Stage Concepts

cards.title: Who Can Be Covered Under a Family Floater Policy?
cards.content: A Family Floater Policy covers only: (1) Spouse, (2) Dependent Children, (3) Parents, (4) Parents-in-law. Extended relatives such as Maternal Uncle, Aunt, Cousins, etc., CANNOT be covered under a Family Floater Policy.

cards.title: When Are Past Savings Most Needed?
cards.content: A person appreciates (needs) their past savings most during the Post-Retirement stage. After retirement, there is no active income, and all expenses must be met from savings and retirement corpus accumulated over the earning years.

cards.title: Younger Age = Lower Liabilities
cards.content: The younger a person is, the fewer financial liabilities they have. Liabilities increase with age as a person takes on responsibilities such as home loans, children's education, and family expenses.

cards.title: Risk Appetite at Young Age = HIGH
cards.content: A young person who has just started earning, with low liabilities and a long time horizon, has a HIGH risk appetite. They can afford to take more financial risk because they have time to recover from potential losses. Note: The correct answer per IC-38 syllabus is HIGH — consistent with the Aggressive risk profile at young age (covered in Financial Planning chapter).

cards.title: When Should You Take Life Insurance?
cards.content: Since the timing of death is uncertain and unpredictable, a person should take life insurance at an Early Age. The earlier you take insurance, the lower the premium and the longer the protection period.

cards.title: What Does Pooling of Risk Mean?
cards.content: Pooling of Risk in insurance means: All similar risks are pooled (grouped) together. When many people facing the same type of risk (e.g., life risk) transfer their individual risks to one insurer, those similar risks are pooled. This allows the insurer to predict losses more accurately and compensate those who suffer actual losses.

sections.title: 🚀 Exam Pro-Tips (Quick Memory)
items: HLV = Human Life Value. Concept introduced by Professor S.S. Huebner.
Air and Sunlight are NOT assets — they are natural gifts, freely available to all.
Three risks in life: Dying Too Early, Living Too Long, Living with Disability.
Natural Wear and Tear = NOT a risk category, NOT covered by insurance.
Life Insurance = Contract of ASSURANCE. General Insurance = Contract of INDEMNITY. Never reverse these.
Mortality is DIRECTLY related to Age — older age = higher premium.
Cash Value Insurance: Advantages = Safe Investment, Saving Discipline, Tax Benefit. Disadvantage = Lower Yields.
Family Floater Policy covers: Spouse, Children, Parents, Parents-in-law. NOT extended relatives like Maternal Uncle.
Post-Retirement = stage when past savings are most needed.
Young age = HIGH risk appetite (Aggressive). Near retirement = LOW risk appetite (Conservative).
Take Life Insurance at an Early Age because death timing is uncertain.
Pooling of Risk = All similar risks grouped together with the insurer.
Subsidy is NOT an element of life insurance business.
NOT an advantage of Cash Value Insurance = Lower Yields. NOT an asset = Air and Sunlight.
